items_missed: The caller's name was never obtained. She was on the phone for eight minutes, she is the person paying ('I'm paying, I like, I'll pay for that'), and she had to ask him his name rather than the reverse ('So, what was your name again?'). The only name captured was the daughter's, pulled off the existing online form. There is no record of who actually called.

No agenda statement and no 'sound good?'. He went from 'Okay, gotcha' to a full pricing monologue inside the first thirty seconds of the call, before establishing a single fact about the move himself.
Availability for the date was never confirmed. 'right now I have it for a Friday' implies a held slot but nobody ever said the 30th is open.

Addresses were never asked — not the origin, not the destination, not a zip code at either end. Everything Landon knows about geography came from the caller volunteering it: '27 miles away from forward to Dallas.' He built a price and sent a quote without ever confirming where the truck is going.

Home size was never independently established. The caller told him the online form was wrong — 'she got some ridiculous quote from something and I'm not sure she's answering the questions, right? Because when they do square footage, she's in a two bedroom apartment now but it's only half her stuff' — and Landon agreed with the diagnosis ('sometimes systems, the system will like relate it as just a StraightUp two bedroom apartment') without ever re-collecting the correct inputs. He identified a bad estimate and then produced a new one from the same missing information.

Stairs, floors and elevators never asked — and this is the most consequential gap on the call, because the caller described both ends in detail and got no follow-up. Origin: 'we would park like the U-Haul out on the back end and then walk under the garage, into the garage and then into the elevator and up.' Destination: 'her floor is the garage floor but I'm sure they have a move-in area or something.' Two elevator buildings, a garage-level approach at one end, and an unknown floor at the other. Landon's entire response was 'Oh, nice' followed by an assumption: 'Typically with the high-rise units they're going to have like a freight elevator and like a loading area and all that kind of stuff for us.' Freight elevators in high-rises usually have to be reserved, and most buildings require a certificate of insurance before they will let a crew in. None of that was asked.
Additional rooms never asked — no garage, storage unit, patio or balcony question.

Special considerations never asked. The caller volunteered the single most fragile item on the job herself — 'she has one big floor length mirror, you all would wrap that for her' — and it never became a question about walls, corners, or elevator dimensions.
Packing needs never asked. The caller assumed it ('as long as she gets everything boxed up') and Landon never confirmed it or offered the service.
Box count never asked. 'some boxes' and 'a lot of ikea bags' is the entire inventory precision on a job quoted at the minimum.
Access concerns never asked — no parking, no loading dock, no move-in reservation, no COI, at either of two elevator buildings.

The moving-stressor question was never asked. The caller told him twice that she and her husband will be out of the country and cannot help ('we're going to be out of out of the country. So we can't help her'), which is a stated anxiety about leaving her daughter alone with this, and it never became a question.
What's-included was only partial: 'we pad and wrap, we disassemble reassemble anything like that you guys need us to do. It's all built-in.' No gas, no truck, no taxes, no insurance, no tools named.

Trip fee never addressed. This move crosses the metroplex — the caller herself said '27 miles away from forward to Dallas' and Landon later called it 'like a forty minute drive.' Whether that is inside the free service zone or carries a transportation fee was never stated in either direction, and it is a material line item on a $515 quote.

No Worries Damage Coverage never mentioned. The caller named a floor-length mirror and a bed she assembled herself and is anxious about ('if you're gonna take this apart, you need to take a picture of it first, get blue tape'). She is handing over the two most breakable things on the job and was never told Einstein covers up to $2,000 to repair, replace or reimburse.

Meet Your Mover never mentioned — and this is the best Meet Your Mover setup in the entire week's sample. The caller is leaving the country, her daughter is receiving the crew alone, and the caller's whole posture on the call is making sure her daughter is looked after. The pre-move email with the crew's names and photos is the exact answer to that, and it was never said.

The clock explanation never said when the clock starts. The 2.5-hour minimum and fifteen-minute proration landed; the on-site contract trigger did not — which matters on a forty-minute cross-metro drive where the caller would reasonably wonder whether she is paying for the drive.
No sense-check anywhere across the pricing, the clock, or the estimate.
No typical time range was given for the home size. The 2.5-hour minimum was asserted without any benchmark for a partial two-bedroom.
Truck count never stated.
Walk distance never asked at either end, across two buildings where the approach runs through a garage and up an elevator.

Save Your Ass speech entirely absent — 0/10. The caller asked twice, in effect, how to make this cheaper, and described a family that already does its own moving ('I basically move all the time myself,' 'we moved in in about two hours ourselves'). The answer she got was a $30 weekday discount. No prep-saves-money framing, no consolidation examples, no carload tip — on a customer who was actively volunteering that the load is mostly ikea bags and boxes she could move herself.

No booking attempt. Landon punted it entirely: 'If you at any point if you guys do decide that you want to get on the schedule, you can give us a call back or you can just respond to this email.' The caller was sold — she said of the disassembly 'that's worth $200 right there, I'm telling you' — she was the payer, and she was asking him to close ('can you send a quote to her or something like that and then I'll talk with her'). There was no offer to hold the 30th, no 'it costs nothing to lock it in and you can still change it,' no specific follow-up time.

No bolded-details framing and no 'reply with any corrections' verification ask. 'you can just respond to this email' was offered as a booking channel, not a request to check the details — which matters more than usual, because the quote is going to the daughter, who was not on this call and has never heard any of these numbers explained.
No hours and no direct number — 'Just reach back out if you have any questions at all we'll be here.'
The caller's name was used zero times, and the daughter's only while reading back the email address.
top_strength: Landon builds trust faster than anyone else in this week's sample, and he does it by leading with the one thing that answers the caller's actual objection. She opened by telling him the online quote was wrong and she did not trust the inputs; his first substantive line went straight at that: 'for us so it's super simple with us. We're just time based. We don't have any like, cause I totally understand that sometimes systems, the system will like relate it as just a StraightUp two bedroom apartment.' He is the only rep this week to use the 'super simple' opener, and he used it to reframe a bad automated quote rather than to introduce a rate sheet. He then hit the moment the whole call turns on. She asked 'you'll put, you'll disassemble the bed and put it back together' and he said 'Yes ma'am. Yeah, we do all of that' — and she answered 'You know what, that's worth $200 right there, I'm telling you I didn't, I'm the one that assembled it.' That is a customer pricing the differentiator herself, out loud, higher than it costs. He reinforced it later without being asked, on the mirror: 'we've had and wrap everything with our moving blankets and that's also just built-in so there's no additional cost for any of that stuff. But that's part of our just standard practice.' He also volunteered money the customer had not asked for: 'the one thing I did want to ask you guys it, it's not like a drastic savings but if you guys did have any flexibility to go from right now I have it for a Friday. If you all were able to do a Thursday or a day during the week, it would be about $30 cheaper' — and when she came back to it at the end confused about whether it was $30 total or per hour, he broke it down cleanly and completely: 'the rates for that day it drops from the $103 per mover to $97 an hour per mover, so it brings a overall hourly rate from $515 to 485.' The On-Time Guarantee was delivered unprompted and in plain language, off the back of the arrival window: 'we just have like a thirty minute arrival window for any traffic. But other than that we have an on time guarantee. So I was just saying if we don't make it within that agreed upon time, we actually start discounting to move from the start cause we just know that can be pretty inconveniencing.' And the rapport was genuine — he asked about the origin of the daughter's name, heard the adoption story, and the caller ended the call saying 'I really appreciate it. Thank you so much.'
coaching_note: Highest-leverage fix: Landon sold this caller completely and then did not ask for anything. She told him the disassembly alone was worth $200 to her, she is the one paying, her daughter is out of the loop, and she explicitly asked him to send something so she could move it forward. The close he needed was: 'Absolutely, I'll send it to her right now. One thing that'll make this easier — there's no deposit and no cancellation fee, so I can put the 30th on the books for her today at zero cost. If you two decide differently after you talk, you just call me and it comes off. Want me to hold it?' That does four things this call missed: it attempts the booking, it uses the no-deposit differentiator he already knows, it removes the risk from the decision-maker who is about to leave the country, and it protects a date on a move that is six weeks out. Instead the entire close was 'if you guys do decide that you want to get on the schedule, you can give us a call back.' Second priority, and this is the structural problem: the probe came in at 2/9. Landon never asked for an address, a floor, a box count, a walk distance, or a single access question — on a move between two elevator buildings where the caller described a garage-level approach at one end and did not know the floor at the other. He identified that the online quote was wrong because the inputs were wrong, and then produced his own quote from even fewer inputs. Warmth is doing all the work on this call and it cannot carry an estimate. Estimate-accuracy flag for the bottom-4 review: he quoted the bare 2.5-hour minimum, $515, and flagged the risk himself before dismissing it — 'the main thing is the drive with it being forty, like a forty minute drive, but even then I still think you guys are gonna fall within that two and a half hour minimum.' A forty-minute loaded drive plus the return, a bed disassembly and reassembly, a floor-length mirror to wrap, a TV, a console, a dresser, three bar stools, boxes and 'a lot of ikea bags,' out of an elevator building and into a high-rise — that is not a 2.5-hour move. This is the apartment-underestimate half of the accuracy problem stated out loud on the recording, and it is the one that ends with an angry customer on move day rather than a padded invoice. The fix is the same in both directions: never quote the minimum without an upper bound and the reason. 'With the drive and the bed I'd expect three to three and a half, so somewhere between $515 and $720 — you only pay for what we use.' Third, the two differentiators he skipped were the two this call was built for. The mirror and the hand-assembled bed are a No Worries conversation. A mother leaving the country while her daughter receives a crew alone is a Meet Your Mover conversation, and it is a better answer to her anxiety than anything else available. Finally, worth naming the good habit so it does not get lost: the On-Time Guarantee delivery here is the cleanest in the batch — volunteered, attached to the arrival window, and explained in terms of why the customer would care. That is the model for how the other two should sound.
phone_presence_notes: Real warmth and real curiosity — 'Totally, get it,' 'Yeah, you're good,' and he asked about the origin of the daughter's name and listened to the adoption story without rushing past it, ending with the caller saying 'I really appreciate it. Thank you so much' — but the score stops at 4 because he never used her name once (he never got it), and the rapport substituted for discovery rather than opening it up: she volunteered the garage approach, the elevators and the floor-length mirror and each one drew an 'Oh, nice' instead of a question.
